description: We are a team of university students from Germany, bringing together computer science, artificial intelligence, cyber security, and aerospace engineering. We came together because we share one goal: to take on "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" and turn two sometimes conflicting satellite records into one consistent, trustworthy view of active fires.
summary:
La Brasa (Spanish for "the ember", the glowing coals that stay hot after the flames are gone) is an open-source web app for firefighters and operations planners in Spain and Portugal. Like an ember, a wildfire can look quiet from space and still be burning.

What did we develop?
La Brasa is an open-source web app for firefighters and operations planners in Spain and Portugal. It builds on 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire data (MODIS and VIIRS). We harmonised all four instruments onto one scale and added an interactive map with a time slider, fire events, drawn areas, a cloud-cover layer and a 10-day fire forecast.

How does it address the challenge?
- Changing sensors: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS datasets
- Clouds: A satellite can't see fires under clouds, so "no fire" can be wrong. La Brasa uses cloud cover at the overpass times to mark fires that were probably hidden. It shows no estimated fire counts.
- Usability: Raw hotspots become fire events, regional time series and a forecast, with their uncertainty shown, so users can explore them in a browser.

Why is it important?
Crews and equipment have to be placed before fires grow. Planners need data they can trust, with its limits shown openly. Because the project is open source (Apache 2.0) and built on public data, other regions can reuse it.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Orbital-Fire-Watch/La-Brasa

La Brasa: Project Information

What it does / how it works

La Brasa is a web app that shows where NASA satellites detected active fires in Spain and Portugal. It answers three questions: how the current fire situation compares with the past, how the fire season is developing, and what the next 10 days look like. It combines 26 years of NASA FIRMS hotspot data (MODIS Terra/Aqua since 2000; VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 since 2012) into one series that can be compared across all years. It runs automatically every day: new FIRMS data is downloaded, cleaned, harmonised, loaded into a database and turned into a fire danger forecast.

Features

26 Years of Comparable Fire Data

  • MODIS → VIIRS harmonisation: every detection converted into "VIIRS equivalents" using a calibrated factor for each region
  • 17 conversion methods tested (monthly factors, Poisson models, gradient boosting, quantile mapping and more): one factor per region was the most accurate
  • Uncertainty shown with every value: 50 % and 90 % error bands from a cross-validated error model
  • Reliability label for every value: measured / converted solid / converted rough
  • MODIS orbit drift detected: no MODIS data used after 2021
  • Static heat sources (industry, gas flares) removed with a location mask learned from the archive
  • VIIRS satellites averaged, not added up, so the series does not double when NOAA-20 joins in 2018
  • Weight per hotspot: the sum over any area you draw matches the harmonised total exactly

Fires Hidden by Clouds

  • Cloud cover at the times the satellites pass over, shown for every day and every area
  • Probably hidden fires marked on the map: seen the day before and the day after, missing on a cloudy day in between
  • Display only: fire counts are never estimated or filled in

10-Day Fire Danger Forecast

  • Probability of a big-fire day (≥ 100 MW) for each region, days 1–10
  • Weeks 2–4 outlook: calmer / usual / riskier than usual
  • Inputs: current fire activity, ECMWF weather forecasts and the Fire Weather Index (FWI) system
  • Confidence range from the 51-member ECMWF weather ensemble
  • A model is only shown if it beats the seasonal average on years it never saw during training; otherwise the seasonal average is shown
  • Day 1: AUC 0.94, better than the seasonal average in all 15 years tested

Fire Events and Their Development

  • Fire event rule: hotspots at most 2 H3 cells (≈ 1.8 km) and at most 2 days apart, at least 2 hotspots per event
  • Status for each fire: new, active for X days, ended
  • Trend for each fire: growing / stable / shrinking
  • Fire list sortable by intensity (FRP), area, duration, hotspots, start or last seen
  • Strongest fire of the period, one click to show it on the map

Map and Analysis

  • Full-screen map with H3 hexagons that get finer as you zoom in, down to single hotspots
  • Choose a country or region, or draw your own area (rectangle, circle, polygon, freehand)
  • Plain comparisons: "3.2 × the usual for this time of year", "rank 2 of 26"
  • "Unusual" view: map coloured red (more than usual) or blue (less than usual)
  • Season phase: before season, rising, peak, declining, after season
  • Season curve compared with the median and the typical range of all years
  • Year overview of 26 years as a heatmap or ring calendar
  • Time slider covering 60 days before and after the reference date
  • MODIS and VIIRS side by side on synchronised maps with one shared colour scale
  • CSV export of hotspots for any selection

Accessibility and Usability

  • Available in English, Spanish and Portuguese, the languages of the affected region
  • Colour-blind-safe palettes (Cividis/Viridis, Okabe-Ito for the satellites)
  • Dark, light and high-contrast themes
  • Adjustable text size and a reduced-motion option
  • Every control works with the keyboard, buttons have screen-reader labels, and colour is never the only way information is shown
  • Guided tutorial with a real example (Galicia, August 2025), built for keyboard and screen-reader use
  • An ⓘ explanation next to every value, saying how it is computed
  • Any view can be shared by link: the full view state is stored in the URL
  • Uses free, open data only, with no account or API key needed

Benefits

La Brasa turns raw satellite detections into answers people can act on. Instead of a cloud of red dots, users see whether the current situation is normal or exceptional, how sure the data is, and what the coming days may bring. Because we harmonised the full 26-year record, long-term trends in fire activity can be analysed without the false jumps caused by new satellites. Marking fires hidden by clouds and showing an uncertainty for every number keeps users from reading too much into gaps or small numbers. Any region or self-drawn area can be analysed and exported in seconds, with no knowledge of satellite products needed.

Intended impact

We want to make NASA's fire data usable for the people who live with wildfires on the Iberian Peninsula: local authorities, emergency planners, journalists, researchers and residents. A clear comparison with past years and a 10-day outlook can help with planning resources and raising awareness before the peak of the fire season, not just during it. By being open about what the data can and cannot show, we want to build trust in satellite data. Our harmonisation method is documented and reproducible, and can be applied to other fire-prone regions of the world.

What makes our project creative

The core idea is to treat the change in satellite fleets as a problem we can measure and correct, not just accept. Most fire maps show raw detections; we rebuilt the history so that years from different satellite eras can be compared fairly. We addressed the blind spot of cloud cover, which the challenge names as an open problem, by marking fires that were probably hidden instead of inventing numbers. The forecast follows a "prove it or don't show it" rule, so a simple, honest seasonal baseline wins over a model that only looks impressive.

Above all, we built La Brasa for everyone, not only for remote sensing experts. Complex statistics become plain statements such as "3.2 × the usual", "rank 2 of 26" or "Peak phase", and a guided tutorial walks new users through a real fire. Three languages, colour-blind-safe palettes, high contrast, adjustable text size, keyboard control and screen-reader support mean that as many people as possible can use satellite fire data, whatever their background or abilities.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Data Sources

  • NASA FIRMS: MODIS Collection 6.1; VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (archive and near real time)
  • Weather: ERA5, ECMWF IFS forecasts and the 51-member ECMWF ensemble (via Open-Meteo)
  • Cloud cover: Meteomatics
  • Region boundaries: Eurostat NUTS-2 (2021)

Languages

  • Python: data pipeline, harmonisation, forecast, backend
  • TypeScript: frontend
  • SQL: PostgreSQL

Data Processing and Modelling

  • pandas, NumPy, SciPy, DuckDB, PyArrow/Parquet
  • H3 (Uber's hexagonal grid system), Shapely
  • Penalised logistic regression with Platt calibration, multinomial logistic regression, bootstrap evaluation
  • Fire Weather Index (FWI) system

Backend and Database

  • FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn
  • PostgreSQL 17 (psycopg)

Frontend

  • React 19, Vite
  • MapLibre GL with OpenFreeMap and Esri satellite imagery
  • h3-js, d3

Infrastructure and Quality

  • Docker Compose, Caddy
  • Linux server (4 vCores, 8 GB RAM) with a daily cron job
  • pytest, Vitest and ESLint; automated KPI checks for the harmonisation and the forecast

SI Assistance

  • Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic), used as declared in SI-USAGE.md
